openers.title: Water Won't Boil at Room Temperature
openers.question: A beaker of water sits on the bench at 25 °C. It evaporates slowly but never boils, and a pressure sensor above it never sees 1 atm of water vapor. What does the sign of ΔG° for turning liquid water into vapor at 1 atm, at 25 °C, tell you?
openers.model_answer: H₂O(l) → H₂O(g): ΔH° = +44.01 kJ; ΔS° = +118.8 J/K = 0.1188 kJ/K; ΔG° = 44.01 − 298 × 0.1188 = +8.6 kJ (from ΔG°f: +8.5 kJ). Positive ΔG°: forming vapor at 1 atm, the standard state, is nonspontaneous at 25 °C. Water evaporates only until its vapor pressure is reached. (OpenStax Example 16.7.)
openers.target: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°, or ΣνΔG°f; its sign predicts spontaneity under standard conditions.

media.credit: AI image made by the instructor with Gemini

openers.title: The Hand Warmer
openers.question: A disposable hand warmer is a pouch of iron powder. Open it and air slowly turns the iron to iron(III) oxide, and a thermometer in the pouch reads about 50 °C for hours. Which two quantities decide the sign of ΔG° for the iron's reaction with oxygen, and which one wins here?
openers.model_answer: 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃: ΔH° = −1648.4 kJ (strongly exothermic); ΔS° = −550.0 J/K (gas consumed). ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = −1648.4 − 298 × (−0.5500) = −1484.5 kJ, matching ΣνΔG°f (−1484.4 kJ). Enthalpy wins: the large negative ΔH° outweighs the entropy penalty, and the released enthalpy warms the hands.
openers.target: ΔG° combines ΔH° and −TΔS°; for strongly exothermic reactions ΔH° dominates.

media.credit: AI image made by the instructor with Gemini

openers.title: Diamonds Are Not Forever
openers.question: Thermodynamically, diamond should turn into graphite at room temperature. Yet a diamond ring shows no change in a lifetime: an X-ray diffractometer still sees a perfect diamond lattice. What does ΔG° say about this change, and what does it not say?
openers.model_answer: C(diamond) → C(graphite): ΔG° = −2.9 kJ by both routes, so the change is spontaneous. ΔG° says nothing about rate: converting diamond's covalent network requires an enormous activation energy, so the change is immeasurably slow.
openers.target: A negative ΔG° means spontaneous, not fast; thermodynamics does not predict rates.

media.credit: AI image made by the instructor with Gemini

openers.title: Zinc from Its Ore
openers.question: Zinc sulfide ore does not break down into zinc and sulfur on its own. A chemist tries pairing that breakdown with the reaction of hydrogen and sulfur to make hydrogen sulfide, but a gas sensor in the reactor finds no hydrogen sulfide at room temperature. How do the free energies of two coupled reactions combine, and why does this pairing fail?
openers.model_answer: ΔG° values add: ZnS → Zn + S, +201.3 kJ; H₂ + S → H₂S, −33.4 kJ; coupled ZnS + H₂ → Zn + H₂S, +167.9 kJ > 0: nonspontaneous. A coupled reaction runs only when the favorable step's ΔG° outweighs the unfavorable one, as for HgO with carbon (−277.4 kJ). (OpenStax Example 16.9.)
openers.target: ΔG° values of coupled reactions add; the sum's sign decides spontaneity.
